To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nurses' perceptions of rewards are influenced by the reward category, their age, and the amount of experience they have in the job.
nurses value both financial and non-financial (psychological) rewards, but that financial rewards are not necessarily more important.
nurses value financial and non-financial and especially psychological rewards, and that the rewarding potential of financial, non-finical and psychological rewards is not significantly different.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of nurses' reward perceptions and the categorization of these rewards.
nurses' reward perceptions and the categorization of rewards in a Belgian context.
the identification of nurses' rewards and the categorization of these rewards.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the establishment of a good reward system for nurses is not a simple matter.
a combination of different types of rewards is the most appropriate strategy to motivate and retain nurses.
the reward system should include a mix of financial, non-finatural and psychological rewards.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nurses' reward perceptions should be taken into account by the hospital manager when designing a reward system.
a reward system for nurses should not only focus on financial rewards, but should also include non-financial and/or psychological rewards.
a reward system for nurses should not only be financially attractive but should also be tailored to nurses' individual preferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rewarding potential of non-financial and especially psychological rewards should be taken into account.
nurses value rewards that are not necessarily linked to their monthly pay.
hospital managers should be more attentive to the non-financial rewards, as these seem to be of great importance for nurses.
